title: Why Do Exams Make Us Anxious?
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Mutiso et al.; Mugotitsa et al.; National Health Service (NHS)
in_text_citation: (Mutiso et al., 2023; Mugotitsa et al., 2025; NHS, 2023a)
content:
Examinations are an important part of university life, but they can also become a major source of emotional pressure. Students may worry about failing, disappointing their families, losing scholarships or falling behind their classmates. These concerns can make examinations feel much bigger than the academic assessment itself.

A Kenyan study involving 9,741 students found that stress was associated with several challenges, including financial difficulties, family-related concerns and uncertainty about the future (Mutiso et al., 2023). Further research among Kenyan university students also highlights how family support systems and academic transitions shape emotional wellbeing during university years (Mugotitsa et al., 2025). This demonstrates that academic stress does not always come from coursework alone; students may be managing several pressures simultaneously.

It is important to recognise that experiencing some nervousness before an examination is not necessarily a sign that something is wrong. The difficulty arises when worry becomes overwhelming and interferes with concentration, sleep or everyday activities (NHS, 2023a).

What can you do?
- Identify the specific examination topics worrying you.
- Divide large revision tasks into smaller sections.
- Practise answering past examination questions.
- Avoid measuring your preparation against other students.
- Speak to someone you trust when the pressure becomes difficult to manage.

Remember, an examination measures your performance in a particular assessment. It does not determine your entire potential or future.

title: How to Create a Revision Plan Without Overwhelming Yourself
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: National Health Service (NHS); Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation (Ofqual)
content:
Looking at an entire semester's workload can make studying feel impossible. When students think about every unfinished assignment, chapter and upcoming examination simultaneously, they may struggle to decide where to begin.

A practical revision plan helps transform a large workload into smaller, manageable activities. The NHS recommends developing realistic study schedules, organising topics into manageable sections and including regular breaks (NHS, 2023b; Ofqual, 2025).

You do not need a complicated timetable to get started.

Try this simple approach:
- Write down the subjects you need to revise.
- Identify the topics you understand least.
- Give each topic a realistic time allocation.
- Set one achievable goal for every study session.
- Include short breaks and time for rest.
- Review your progress at the end of the day.

For example, instead of writing "Study database management", choose "Revise database normalisation and attempt three practice questions".

BEGANI tip: Use the Study & Focus Pomodoro timer to divide your revision into focused sessions. Start with 25 minutes of studying followed by a five-minute break.

Your objective is not to complete everything in one sitting. It is to make consistent progress.
references:
National Health Service. (2023b). Tips on preparing for exams. https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/children-and-young-adults/help-for-teenagers-young-adults-and-students/tips-on-preparing-for-exams/

title: The Fear of Failure – When Academic Expectations Become Too Much
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation (Ofqual)
content:
For some students, the fear of failing becomes more stressful than the examination itself.

You may feel that one poor grade will disappoint your parents, affect your career opportunities or make you appear less capable than your classmates. These expectations can create pressure to perform perfectly, even when perfection is unrealistic.

Fear-based thinking can also make students avoid revision. Someone who is afraid of discovering that they do not understand a topic may postpone studying altogether.

Ofqual (2025) highlights how negative beliefs about examination outcomes can contribute to anxiety. Replacing extreme predictions with more balanced and realistic thoughts can help students approach assessments differently.

Try changing your internal conversation:
- Instead of "If I fail, my future is finished", try "This examination matters, but there are still opportunities to improve."
- Instead of "Everyone understands this except me", try "I need more practice with this particular topic."
- Instead of "I must get everything right", try "I will prepare as well as I reasonably can."

A small exercise: Write down one academic worry and then identify what you can realistically do about it today.

Your worth is not dependent on maintaining perfect grades. Learning includes mistakes, improvement and trying again.

title: How to Manage Anxiety on Examination Day
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
The examination day can bring a mixture of excitement, nervousness and uncertainty. Even students who have prepared adequately may experience a racing heartbeat, sweaty palms or difficulty concentrating.

The key is to focus on what you can control rather than trying to eliminate every feeling of nervousness.

The NHS recommends preparing examination materials in advance, arriving with sufficient time and using breathing exercises when feeling overwhelmed (NHS, 2023b).

Before entering the examination room:
- Prepare your pens, identification and other required materials.
- Eat something appropriate and drink water.
- Avoid last-minute comparisons with classmates.
- Take a few slow, comfortable breaths.
- Remind yourself that you only need to handle one question at a time.

During the examination:
- Read the instructions carefully.
- Identify questions you can answer confidently.
- Allocate time according to the marks available.
- Return to difficult questions after completing easier ones.
- Avoid panicking if your mind temporarily goes blank.

After the examination, allow yourself to move on. Repeatedly analysing every answer with classmates can increase unnecessary worry.

An examination is one event. Give yourself permission to focus on the next step.
references: National Health Service. (2023b). Tips on preparing for exams. https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/children-and-young-adults/help-for-teenagers-young-adults-and-students/tips-on-preparing-for-exams/

title: Understanding Anxiety – When Worry Becomes Overwhelming
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Everyone experiences worry from time to time. Students may feel anxious about examinations, finances, relationships, presentations or decisions about their future.

Anxiety is a normal human response to perceived uncertainty or danger. However, it can become a concern when fear and worry are persistent, difficult to manage and begin interfering with everyday life.

The National Institute of Mental Health explains that anxiety disorders involve more than occasional nervousness. Symptoms can persist and affect different areas of a person's life (National Institute of Mental Health [NIMH], n.d.).

Some experiences associated with anxiety include:
- Constant worrying about possible outcomes.
- Difficulty concentrating.
- Feeling restless or unusually tense.
- Avoiding situations that cause fear.
- Sleep difficulties.
- Physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat.

Experiencing one or more of these symptoms does not automatically mean you have an anxiety disorder.

What might help?
Start by identifying situations that tend to trigger your worry. Try maintaining a regular routine, taking breaks, practising relaxation exercises and speaking with someone you trust.

If anxiety is persistent or interferes with your studies and relationships, consider speaking with a qualified mental-health professional.

You do not have to wait until things become unbearable before seeking support.
references: National Institute of Mental Health. (n.d.). Anxiety disorders. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, National Institutes of Health. https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/anxiety-disorders

title: Breaking the Cycle of Overthinking
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Have you ever spent hours replaying a conversation, worrying about an assignment or imagining everything that could go wrong?

Overthinking can make relatively small concerns feel increasingly difficult to manage. Instead of helping you find solutions, repeatedly analysing the same situation may leave you mentally exhausted.

The World Health Organization's stress-management guide introduces practical approaches such as noticing difficult thoughts, grounding yourself in the present and responding to yourself with kindness (World Health Organization [WHO], 2020).

Try the following exercise:
- Identify the thought occupying your attention.
- Ask yourself whether it describes something happening now or something you fear might happen.
- Consider whether there is an action you can take.
- If there is, identify one manageable next step.
- If there is not, gently redirect your attention to an activity in the present.

For example, worrying repeatedly about an examination result that has not yet been released will not change the outcome.

You could instead take a walk, prepare for your next class or spend time with someone you enjoy being around.

Remember, having a thought does not mean it is a prediction or a fact.
references: World Health Organization. (2020). Doing what matters in times of stress: An illustrated guide. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240003927

title: Grounding Exercises – Bringing Your Attention Back to the Present
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Sometimes stress and anxiety make it difficult to concentrate on what is happening around you. Your attention may become occupied by worries about the past or possible future events.

Grounding is a technique that helps redirect attention towards your immediate surroundings and present experience.

The WHO includes grounding among the practical techniques in its guide for managing stress (WHO, 2020).

Try the 5–4–3–2–1 exercise:
- 5 things: Identify five things you can see.
- 4 things: Notice four things you can physically feel.
- 3 things: Identify three sounds around you.
- 2 things: Notice two things you can smell.
- 1 thing: Identify one thing you can taste.

Move through the exercise slowly without rushing to complete it.

You can also try:
- Feeling your feet resting on the floor.
- Noticing the movement of your breathing.
- Describing objects around you.
- Listening carefully to the sounds in your environment.

Grounding is not a cure for anxiety, but it can be a useful self-management technique.

references: World Health Organization. (2020). Doing what matters in times of stress: An illustrated guide. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240003927

title: When Anxiety Shows Up Physically
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH); World Health Organization (WHO)
content:
Anxiety is not experienced only through thoughts and emotions. It can also involve physical reactions.

A student preparing for an examination may notice a faster heartbeat, muscle tension, sweating, stomach discomfort or changes in breathing.

These reactions are part of the body's response to perceived stress. However, physical symptoms can have other causes, so they should not automatically be attributed to anxiety.

The NIMH explains that anxiety disorders can involve both psychological and physical symptoms, with their severity and effects varying between individuals (NIMH, n.d.).

Ways to support yourself:
- Pause and identify what you are experiencing.
- Find a comfortable position.
- Try gentle, slow breathing without forcing or holding your breath.
- Take a short walk if appropriate.
- Reduce excessive caffeine if it makes you feel more unsettled.
- Consider discussing persistent symptoms with a healthcare professional.

If you experience severe, sudden or unexplained physical symptoms, seek medical assessment rather than assuming they are caused by anxiety.

Your physical wellbeing deserves attention just as much as your academic performance.

title: Academic Burnout – When Studying Starts Feeling Exhausting
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Chong et al.; Kaggwa et al.
content:
University life often involves demanding coursework, examinations, assignments, personal responsibilities and expectations about the future.

When academic pressure continues without sufficient opportunities for recovery, students may experience persistent exhaustion, disengagement from their studies and a reduced sense of academic effectiveness.

Research on student burnout identifies these experiences as important dimensions of academic burnout (Chong et al., 2025; Kaggwa et al., 2021).

Burnout should not be confused with an ordinary tiring day. It generally involves a more persistent pattern of difficulty.

You might notice:
- Feeling exhausted even after completing routine tasks.
- Losing interest in subjects you previously enjoyed.
- Struggling to concentrate on assignments.
- Feeling disconnected from academic activities.
- Doubting your ability to complete your studies.

These experiences can have different causes and do not establish a diagnosis.

What can you do?
Start by identifying what is consuming most of your energy. Review your workload, introduce reasonable study limits and allow yourself time away from academic responsibilities.

If the exhaustion continues, consider speaking with a university counsellor or healthcare professional.

You deserve a sustainable academic experience, not one built entirely around exhaustion.

title: Five Warning Signs That You May Need an Academic Reset
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Sometimes students become so accustomed to being busy that they fail to notice when their wellbeing is deteriorating.

Recognising changes in your habits and emotional state can help you respond before difficulties become more disruptive.

Research reviewing student burnout identifies academic demands and other personal and environmental factors as contributors to student exhaustion (Chong et al., 2025).

Here are five experiences worth paying attention to:
- Constant exhaustion: You regularly feel drained by academic responsibilities.
- Loss of motivation: Activities that once interested you now feel difficult to approach.
- Difficulty concentrating: You struggle to remain focused on ordinary study tasks.
- Emotional irritability: You find yourself becoming frustrated more easily.
- Feeling ineffective: You increasingly doubt your ability to accomplish academic tasks.

These are not diagnostic criteria, and they can also occur for other reasons.

Consider an academic reset:
- Reassess your current workload.
- Identify tasks that can be postponed or prioritised.
- Take meaningful breaks.
- Reconnect with supportive people.
- Seek assistance if your difficulties persist.

Recognising that you need support is not a failure. It is an opportunity to respond to your needs.

title: Rest Is Not Laziness – Why Students Need Recovery Time
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Many students feel guilty when they are not studying. They may believe that every free moment should be spent revising, completing assignments or preparing for examinations.

However, continuously working without adequate recovery can make it harder to maintain concentration and emotional balance.

The NHS recommends regular study breaks and physical activity as part of managing examination pressure. It also recognises the importance of taking time away from revision (NHS, 2023b).

Ways to introduce recovery into your routine:
- Take short breaks between study sessions.
- Use the Pomodoro technique if structured sessions help you.
- Listen to relaxing sounds during a break.
- Stretch or take a short walk.
- Spend time with friends and family.
- Protect time for hobbies and activities you enjoy.

Rest does not mean abandoning your responsibilities. It means recognising that your wellbeing is part of your ability to manage them.

BEGANI tip: Use the Study & Focus section to schedule breaks rather than waiting until you are completely exhausted.

You are a student, but you are also a person who needs rest.

title: Why Sleep Matters More Than Another Late-Night Study Session
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
content:
When examinations approach, students sometimes sacrifice sleep to create more revision time.

Although this may appear productive, consistently reducing sleep can affect attention, memory, mood and general wellbeing.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends at least seven hours of sleep per night for adults aged 18–60. Adequate sleep also supports attention, memory and emotional health (CDC, 2024).

Consider these practical changes:
- Establish a reasonably consistent bedtime.
- Avoid leaving all revision until late at night.
- Give yourself time to wind down before sleeping.
- Keep your sleeping environment comfortable.
- Reduce distractions when preparing for bed.

If you have an examination the following morning, prioritise the topics that need the most attention and allow yourself adequate time to rest.

Sleep is not time wasted. It is an important part of looking after your mind and body.

title: The Hidden Cost of All-Night Cramming
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
content:
It can be tempting to spend an entire night revising when an examination is approaching.

You might feel that sleeping means losing valuable preparation time. However, repeated all-night study sessions can leave you tired, distracted and less able to function effectively the following day.

The CDC identifies sufficient sleep as important for attention, memory and emotional wellbeing (CDC, 2024).

Rather than depending on last-minute cramming, try distributing your revision across several days.

A better alternative:
- Identify the topics most likely to need additional practice.
- Divide them into manageable sessions.
- Review previously studied material.
- Attempt practice questions.
- Stop studying at a reasonable time.
- Protect your sleep schedule.

If you are already exhausted, consider whether another hour of revision is more useful than allowing yourself to recover.

Academic preparation should not require repeatedly compromising your health.

title: Building a Healthy Sleep Routine as a University Student
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
content:
University schedules can be unpredictable. Lectures, assignments, social activities and personal responsibilities may make it difficult to maintain consistent sleeping habits.

However, creating a simple routine can make it easier to protect your rest.

The CDC recommends maintaining regular sleeping and waking times, creating a comfortable sleeping environment and reducing electronic device use before bedtime (CDC, 2024).

Try building your own evening routine:
- Finish demanding academic activities before bedtime where possible.
- Prepare your clothes, books and materials for the following day.
- Reduce screen use during the final 30 minutes before sleep.
- Avoid caffeine late in the day if it interferes with your sleep.
- Choose a relaxing activity such as reading or listening to gentle sounds.

If you enjoy rain sounds or guided relaxation, BEGANI's Sleep & Relaxation collection can become part of your wind-down routine.

Remember that sleep needs vary, and persistent difficulties sleeping deserve professional attention.

title: Your Academic Performance Does Not Define Your Worth
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Receiving a disappointing grade can affect your confidence, especially when you have invested considerable time and effort into your studies.

You may begin questioning your abilities or comparing your performance with classmates who appear to be doing better.

However, academic results represent performance in particular assessments. They cannot capture every skill, personal quality or ability you possess.

A study of university students in Kenya explored the relationship between social media use, stress, anxiety and self-perception, highlighting the importance of how students evaluate themselves in relation to others (Oriaso & Waithera, 2025).

When a result disappoints you:
- Give yourself time to process the outcome.
- Identify what went well and what needs improvement.
- Ask for feedback where possible.
- Create a realistic improvement plan.
- Recognise progress beyond examination grades.

You can acknowledge that you need to improve academically without treating yourself as a failure.

Your value as a person is not a number on a results slip.
references: Oriaso, S. O., & Waithera, J. M. (2025). Social media addiction, stress, anxiety, depression, and self-perception among undergraduate students at the University of Nairobi, Kenya. Journal of Medical and Health Sciences, 4(1), 42–51. https://doi.org/10.51317/jmhs.v4i1.800

title: The Pressure of Comparing Your University Journey With Others
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
University life can sometimes feel like a competition.

One student receives an internship, another achieves excellent grades, someone else starts a business, while others appear to have everything figured out.

Seeing these achievements may create the impression that you are falling behind.

However, people have different circumstances, opportunities, responsibilities and timelines. Comparing your progress with someone else's visible achievements can produce an unfair assessment of your own journey.

Research on social comparison among social media users has identified associations between viewing idealised images and changes in self-evaluation (Taylor & Armes, 2024).

Try changing your approach:
- Focus on your own academic and personal goals.
- Celebrate progress, including small improvements.
- Avoid treating another person's success as evidence of your failure.
- Remember that you rarely see the difficulties behind someone's achievements.
- Set goals based on your circumstances and priorities.

You do not need to graduate, secure an internship or achieve every milestone at the same time as your classmates.

Your journey is allowed to look different.
references: Taylor, J., & Armes, G. (2024). Social comparison on Instagram, and its relationship with self-esteem and body-esteem. Discover Psychology, 4, Article 129. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44202-024-00241-3

title: Social Media, Self-Image and the Pressure to Appear Successful
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Social media can help students maintain friendships, discover opportunities and access useful information.

However, it can also expose users to carefully selected images of other people's achievements, lifestyles and appearances.

When students repeatedly compare their everyday experiences with these idealised presentations, they may become dissatisfied with their own circumstances.

Research involving undergraduate students at the University of Nairobi examined associations between social media use, stress, anxiety and self-perception (Oriaso & Waithera, 2025). Other research has explored the relationship between Instagram-based social comparisons and self-esteem or body-esteem (Taylor & Armes, 2024).

Develop a healthier relationship with social media:
- Unfollow accounts that consistently make you feel inadequate.
- Remember that online posts rarely show an entire person's life.
- Avoid measuring your popularity through likes and comments.
- Take breaks when online activity becomes overwhelming.
- Follow accounts that encourage learning, creativity and positive development.

Social media should be a tool for connection and discovery, not a constant measurement of your worth.

title: Small Things You Can Do When Everything Feels Overwhelming
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
There are times when academic and personal responsibilities seem to arrive simultaneously.

You might have an assignment due, examinations approaching, financial concerns and personal responsibilities competing for your attention.

During such moments, trying to solve every problem immediately can make the situation feel even more difficult.

The WHO recommends practical stress-management approaches that include grounding, recognising difficult thoughts, acting according to personal values and practising self-kindness (WHO, 2020).

Try this simple five-step reset:
- Pause: Give yourself a moment before responding to everything at once.
- Breathe: Take a few comfortable, slow breaths.
- Identify: Write down what is worrying you.
- Prioritise: Choose one manageable task to address first.
- Connect: Reach out to someone supportive if you need assistance.

You can also take a short walk, listen to relaxing sounds or use a guided meditation exercise.

Small actions cannot resolve every difficult circumstance, but they can help you approach the next step more calmly.

You do not have to figure everything out today.
references: World Health Organization. (2020). Doing what matters in times of stress: An illustrated guide. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240003927

title: Asking for Help Is Not a Sign of Weakness
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
original_source: Mugotitsa et al.; Wao et al.
content:
Some students avoid asking for help because they fear being judged, misunderstood or viewed as incapable of handling their own problems.

Others believe that their difficulties are not serious enough to deserve attention.

However, seeking support is a reasonable response when personal or academic challenges become difficult to manage. Research among university students in Kenya indicates that strong social and family support acts as an important protective factor for student mental health, whereas navigating challenges without support increases vulnerability (Mugotitsa et al., 2025). Additionally, a 2025 systematic review examining university students across Africa identified barriers to mental-health support, including financial constraints, limited awareness of available services and concerns associated with stigma (Wao et al., 2025).

You can begin by:
- Talking to a trusted friend or family member.
- Contacting your university counselling department.
- Speaking with a lecturer or student welfare representative.
- Seeking guidance from a qualified mental-health professional.

You do not need to have the perfect words to explain what you are experiencing.

You could simply say:
"I have been finding things difficult lately, and I think I need someone to talk to."

Asking for help does not mean you have failed. It means you are taking your wellbeing seriously.
references:

title: Where Can University Students Find Mental Health Support?
author: BEGANI Editorial Team
content:
Knowing that support exists is important, but knowing where to find it can make the difference between continuing to struggle alone and receiving appropriate assistance.

Universities may provide counselling services, student welfare offices, peer-support initiatives and referrals to external healthcare professionals. Research examining Kenyan public universities shows that student counsellors use structured therapeutic approaches—including supportive guidance, stress-management strategies and emotional adjustment counselling—to help students navigate academic and personal challenges (Too & Orao, 2026).

However, a systematic review of mental-health services among university students in Africa identified gaps in awareness, affordability and accessibility, demonstrating the importance of making support pathways easier for students to understand (Wao et al., 2025).

Places to consider when seeking support:
- University counselling services: Ask your institution about available professional counselling.
- Student welfare offices: Find out whether your university offers additional academic or personal support.
- Qualified mental-health professionals: Consider a psychologist, psychiatrist or other appropriate healthcare provider.
- Trusted support networks: Friends, family members and supportive lecturers can help you navigate available services.
- Recognised health organisations: Use reliable mental-health information from organisations such as WHO and NIMH.

If you are experiencing a mental-health emergency or are in immediate danger, seek urgent assistance through local emergency services or the nearest appropriate healthcare facility.

A message to remember:
You do not have to wait until you reach a breaking point to seek support. Getting help early can make it easier to understand what you are experiencing and identify appropriate next steps.
